source_text: Ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τόμῳ τῶν ὑπαγορευθέντων ἡμῖν πρὸς τὸν Κέλσου ἐπιγραφέντα ἀληθῆ λόγον καταλήξαντες εἰς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν προσωποποιΐαν, αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν εἰληφότι, τοῦτον συντάσσειν προαιρούμεθα, ἀπολογούμενοι πρὸς τὰ φερόμενα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐγκλήματα κατὰ τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν πιστευσάντων. καὶ αὐτό γε τοῦτο πρῶτον ἐφίσταμεν, τί δή ποτε ἅπαξ κρίνας προσωποποιεῖν ὁ Κέλσος οὐ προσωποποιεῖ Ἰουδαῖον πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν πιστεύοντας λέγοντα ἀλλὰ πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων· πιθανώτατος δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἔδοξεν ὁ λόγος εἶναι αὐτῷ πρὸς ἡμᾶς γραφόμενος. ἀλλὰ μή ποτε ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελόμενος εἰδέναι τὸ ἀκόλουθον οὐκ εἶδε κατὰ τὸν τόπον τῆς προσωποποιΐας. τί οὖν καὶ λέγει πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων πιστεύοντας, κατανοητέον. φησὶν αὐτοὺς καταλιπόντας τὸν πάτριον νόμον τῷ ἐψυχαγωγῆσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἠπατῆσθαι πάνυ γελοίως καὶ ἀπηυτομοληκέναι εἰς ἄλλο ὄνομα καὶ εἰς ἄλλον βίον, μηδὲ τοῦτο κατανοήσας, ὅτι οἱ ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν πιστεύοντες οὐ καταλελοίπασι τὸν πάτριον νόμον. βιοῦσι γὰρ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν, ἐπώνυμοι τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἐκδοχὴν πτωχείας τοῦ νόμου γεγενημένοι. Ἐβίων τε γὰρ ὁ πτωχὸς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις καλεῖται, καὶ Ἐβιωναῖοι χρηματίζουσιν οἱ ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὡς Χριστὸν παραδεξάμενοι. δεξάμενοι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος δὲ μέχρι πολλοῦ φαίνεται τὰ κατὰ τὸν Μωϋσέως νόμον Ἰουδαϊκὰ ἔθη τετηρηκέναι, ὡς μηδέπω ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ μαθὼν ἀναβαίνειν ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ τὸ γράμμα νόμου ἐπὶ τὸν κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα· ὅπερ ἀπὸ τῶν Πράξεων τῶν ἀποστόλων μεμαθήκαμεν. „τῇ“ γὰρ „ἐπαύριον“ τοῦ ἑωρᾶσθαι ἄγγελον θεοῦ τῷ Κορνηλίῳ, ὑποτιθέμενον αὐτῷ πέμψαι „εἰς Ἰόππην“ ἐπὶ Σίμωνα τὸν καλούμενον Πέτρον, „ἀνέβη Πέτρος εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον προσεύξασθαι περὶ ὥραν ἕκτην. ἐγένετο δὲ πρόσπεινος καὶ ἤθελε γεύσασθαι. παρασκευαζόντων δ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐγένετο ἔκστασις ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν, καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον καὶ καταβαῖνον σκεῦός τι ὡς ὀθόνην μεγάλην, τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς καθιέμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἐν ᾧ ὑπῆρχε πάντα τὰ τετράποδα καὶ ἑρπετὰ τῆς γῆς καὶ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. καὶ ἐγένετο φωνὴ πρὸς αὐτόν· ἀναστὰς, Πέτρε, θῦσον καὶ φάγε. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος εἶπε· μηδαμῶς, κύριε, ὅτι οὐδέ ποτε ἔφαγον πᾶν κοινὸν καὶ ἀκάθαρτον. καὶ φωνὴ ἐκ δευτέρου πρὸς αὐτόν· ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἐκαθάρισε σὺ μὴ κοίνου.“ ὅρα γὰρ ἐν τούτοις, τίνα τρόπον παρίσταται τὰ Ἰουδαϊκὰ ἔθη περὶ καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων ἔτι τηρῶν ὁ Πέτρος. καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἑξῆς δηλοῦται ὅτι ὀπτασίας ἐδεήθη, ἵνα κοινωνήσῃ τῶν λόγων τῆς πίστεως τῷ μὴ κατὰ σάρκα Ἰσραηλίτῃ Κορνηλίῳ καὶ τοῖς σὺν αὐτῷ ὡς ἔτι Ἰουδαῖος καὶ κατὰ τὰς Ἰουδαίων παραδόσεις ζῶν, καταφρονῶν τῶν ἔξω τοῦ ἰουδαϊσμοῦ. καὶ ἐν τῇ πρὸς Γαλάτας δὲ ἐπιστολῇ Παῦλος ἐμφαίνει ὅτι Πέτρος ἔτι φοβούμενος τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, παυσάμενος τοῦ μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνεσθίειν, ἐλθόντος Ἰακώβου πρὸς αὐτὸν „ἀφώριζεν ἑαυτὸν“ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν, „φοβούμενος τοὺς ἐκ τῆς περιτομῆς“· καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ πεποιήκασιν αὐτῷ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Βαρνάβας. καὶ ἀκόλουθόν γε ἦν μὴ ἀποστῆναι τῶν Ἰουδαϊκῶν ἐθῶν τοὺς εἰς τὴν περιτομὴν ἀποσταλέντας, ὅτε „οἱ δοκοῦντες στῦλοι εἶναι δεξιὰς ἔδωκαν Παύλῳ καὶ Βαρνάβᾳ κοινωνίας,“ „αὐτοὶ εἰς τὴν περιτομὴν“ ἀπιόντες, ἵν᾿ ἐκεῖνοι τοῖς ἔθνεσι κηρύξωσι. τί δὲ λέγω ὅτι οἱ κηρύσσοντες „εἰς τὴν περιτομὴν“ ὑπέστελλον ἑαυτοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν καὶ ἀφώριζον; ὅτε καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Παῦλος „τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις Ἰουδαῖος“ ἐγίνετο, „ἵνα Ἰουδαίους“ κερδήσῃ. διὸ, ὡς καὶ ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων γέγραπται, καὶ προσφορὰν προσήνεγκεν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον, ἵνα πείσῃ Ἰουδαίους περὶ τοῦ μὴ εἶναι ἀποστάτης νόμου. ταῦτα δὲ πάντα εἰ ἠπίστατο ὁ Κέλσος, οὐκ ἂν ἐπροσωποποιήσατο τὸν Ἰουδαῖον λέγοντα πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ ἰουδαϊσμοῦ πιστεύοντας τό· τί παθόντες, ὦ πολῖται, κατελίπετε τὸν πάτριον νόμον καὶ ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου, πρὸς ὃν ἄρτι διειλέγμεθα, ψυχαγωγηθέντες πάνυ γελοίως ἐξηπατήθητε καὶ ἀφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀπηυτομολήσατε εἰς ἄλλο ὄνομα καὶ εἰς ἄλλον βίον;
pass_a_gloss: In the first tome (τόμος) of the things dictated (ὑπαγορεύω) by us against Celsus’s [work] entitled True Doctrine (ἀληθὴς λόγος), having ended (καταλήγω) at the Jew’s impersonation (προσωποποιΐα, character-speech) against Jesus, [the tome] having received sufficient compass (αὐτάρκη περιγραφήν), we choose (προαιρέομαι) to compose this [tome], making defence (ἀπολογέομαι) against the charges (ἔγκλημα) brought by him against those from the people of the Jews who believed (πιστεύω) in Jesus. And this first we consider (ἐφίστημι): why ever, having once decided to impersonate, Celsus does not make a Jew speaking to those believing from the nations (ἔθνη) but to those from the Jews; yet the argument (λόγος) would have seemed most persuasive (πιθανός) to him written against us. But perhaps the one professing to know all did not see what is consistent (τὸ ἀκόλουθον) regarding the impersonation. What then he says to believers from the Jews must be considered. He says they, having left the ancestral law (πάτριος νόμος), by being beguiled (ψυχαγωγέω) by Jesus were deceived (ἀπατάω) very laughably (γελοίως) and deserted (αὐτομολέω, ἀπ-) to another name and another life (βίος), not having noticed even this, that those from the Jews believing in Jesus have not left the ancestral law. For they live according to it, having become named after the poverty (πτωχεία) of [their] interpretation (ἐκδοχή) of the law. For Ebion the poor man is called among Jews, and Ebionites are called those from the Jews who accepted (παραδέχομαι) Jesus as Christ. And Peter for a long time appears to have kept (τηρέω) the Jewish customs (ἔθη) according to Moses’ law, as not yet having learned from Jesus to ascend (ἀναβαίνω) from the law according to the letter (γράμμα) to that according to the spirit (πνεῦμα); which we have learned from the Acts of the Apostles. [Quotation Acts 10:9–15: next day after angel of God seen by Cornelius, advising him to send to Joppa for Simon called Peter, Peter went up to the upper room (ὑπερῷον) to pray about the sixth hour; became hungry (πρόσπεινος), wished to taste; while they prepared, ecstasy/trance (ἔκστασις) on him; beholds heaven opened, a vessel (σκεῦος) like a great linen sheet (ὀθόνη) let down by four corners (ἀρχαί) on the earth, in which all quadrupeds, creeping things (ἑρπετά) of earth, birds of heaven; a voice: rise, Peter, sacrifice/kill (θύω) and eat; Peter: by no means, Lord, for never did I eat anything common (κοινός) and unclean (ἀκάθαρτος); voice a second time: what God cleansed (καθαρίζω) do not you make common (κοινόω).] See how Peter is presented still keeping Jewish customs about clean and unclean. From what follows it is shown he needed (δέομαι) a vision (ὀπτασία) in order to share (κοινωνέω) the words of the faith with Cornelius, not an Israelite according to flesh (σάρξ), and those with him, as still a Jew and living by the Jews’ traditions (παράδοσις), despising (καταφρονέω) those outside Judaism (ἰουδαϊσμός). In the epistle to the Galatians Paul shows that Peter, still fearing the Jews, having stopped eating with the nations, James having come to him, separated (ἀφορίζω) himself from the nations, fearing those of the circumcision (περιτομή); the same the remaining Jews and Barnabas did with him. And it was consistent that those sent to the circumcision not depart from Jewish customs, when those reputed to be pillars (στῦλοι) gave right hands of fellowship (κοινωνία) to Paul and Barnabas, themselves going off to the circumcision, so that those might preach (κηρύσσω) to the nations. Why do I say that those preaching to the circumcision drew back (ὑποστέλλω) and separated themselves from the nations, when Paul himself became to Jews a Jew that he might gain (κερδαίνω) Jews? Therefore, as written in the Acts, he brought an offering (προσφορά) to the altar (θυσιαστήριον) to persuade Jews he was not an apostate (ἀποστάτης) from the law. If Celsus had known all this he would not have made the Jew say to believers from Judaism: What having suffered (τί παθόντες), O citizens (πολῖται), did you leave the ancestral law, and, beguiled by that one with whom we just now argued (διαλέγομαι), very laughably were deceived (ἐξαπατάω) and deserted from us to another name and another life?
pass_b_english: In the first book of our dictated reply to Celsus’s work entitled The True Doctrine, we ended at the speech addressed to Jesus that Celsus puts in the mouth of his Jew, since that book had reached a sufficient length. This book we choose to compose, making our defence against the charges he brings against those from the people of the Jews who have believed in Jesus. And this is the very first thing we note: why, having once decided to bring on a character, Celsus does not have his Jew speak to those who believe from among the Gentiles, but to those from among the Jews. Yet his argument would have seemed most persuasive had it been written against us. But perhaps the man who professes to know everything did not see what consistency required in the speech he gave his character.

Let us consider, then, what he says to those from among the Jews who believe. He says that they have left the law of their fathers, that, beguiled by Jesus, they have been quite ridiculously deceived, and that they have deserted to another name and another way of life. He did not even notice that those from among the Jews who believe in Jesus have not left the law of their fathers. For they live by it, and they have come to be named after the poverty of their interpretation of the law. For among the Jews the poor man is called Ebion, and those from among the Jews who have accepted Jesus as the Christ are called Ebionites.

Peter too appears to have kept for a long time the Jewish customs that follow the law of Moses, since he had not yet learned from Jesus to rise from the law according to the letter to the law according to the spirit. This we have learned from the Acts of the Apostles. For on the day after an angel of God had appeared to Cornelius, telling him to send “to Joppa” for Simon called Peter (Acts 10:3–5), “Peter went up to the upper room to pray, about the sixth hour. And he became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing it, a trance came upon him, and he saw heaven opened and a vessel coming down, like a great sheet, let down by its four corners upon the earth; and in it were all the four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth and the birds of the sky. And a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat.’ But Peter said, ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean.’ And a voice came to him a second time: ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common’ ” (Acts 10:9–15).

See in these words how Peter is presented as still keeping the Jewish customs about clean and unclean. And what follows makes clear that he needed a vision so that he would share the words of faith with Cornelius, who was not an Israelite according to the flesh, and with those who were with him; for he was still a Jew, living by the traditions of the Jews and looking down on those outside Judaism (Acts 10:28).

In the Epistle to the Galatians, too, Paul shows that Peter, still afraid of the Jews, stopped eating with the Gentiles, and when James came to him “he separated himself” from the Gentiles, “fearing those of the circumcision”; and the rest of the Jews and Barnabas did the same as he did (Galatians 2:12–13). And it was consistent that those who had been sent to the circumcision should not depart from the Jewish customs, when “those who were reputed to be pillars gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship,” and went off themselves “to the circumcision,” so that those two might preach to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:9).

But why do I say that those who preached “to the circumcision” drew back and separated themselves from the Gentiles, when Paul himself also became “to the Jews a Jew, that he might win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20)? That is why, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, he even brought an offering to the altar, to persuade the Jews that he was not an apostate from the law (Acts 21:21–26).

If Celsus had known all this, he would not have made his Jew say to those from Judaism who believe: “What possessed you, my fellow citizens, to leave the law of your fathers, and, beguiled by that man with whom we were just now arguing, to be so ridiculously deceived, and to desert us for another name and another way of life?”

choices.why: opening: ‘πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν’ now ‘addressed to Jesus’ (was ‘against Jesus’); dropped added ‘now’
‘ἂν ἔδοξεν’ now ‘would have seemed’ (was softened ‘might well have’)
‘τὸ ἀκόλουθον’ now ‘what consistency required’ (was ‘what was fitting’)
causal dative restored: beguiled by Jesus → deceived (was attached to leaving the law)
added missing ‘For’ (γάρ) before the Ebion explanation
‘ἵνα κοινωνήσῃ’ now purpose ‘so that he would share’

translator_notes: Copy-text: staged source_2.json section 1 (Koetschau 2.1); row is complete (ends with Celsus’s question). The staged text reads ‘παραδεξάμενοι. δεξάμενοι.’: a doubled word (dittography or a variant carried into the transcription); translated once. ‘αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν εἰληφότι’ (dative masculine) is taken with τῷ πρώτῳ τόμῳ (the first book had reached sufficient length), not with προσωποποιΐαν. ‘τοῦτον’ = this tome (Book 2). ‘πιθανώτατος δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἔδοξεν ὁ λόγος εἶναι αὐτῷ πρὸς ἡμᾶς γραφόμενος’: ‘us’ = Gentile Christians such as Origen; the sentence is Origen’s concession that an attack on Gentile believers would have been more plausible. The opening report of Celsus’s charge is indirect speech and left without quotation marks; the closing direct quotation is in quotation marks. ‘τί παθόντες’ rendered idiomatically ‘What possessed you’. ‘ἐπώνυμοι τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἐκδοχὴν πτωχείας τοῦ νόμου’: the Ebionites are named for the poverty of their interpretation of the law (Origen’s wordplay on Hebrew ʾebyon, ‘poor’). Acts 10:9: Origen reads ὑπερῷον (‘upper room’) where the New Testament text has δῶμα (‘housetop’); translated as Origen quotes it. ‘θῦσον’ = ‘kill’ (slaughter for food). Galatians 2:12: Origen says ‘when James came to him’ (ἐλθόντος Ἰακώβου), where Paul’s text has ‘certain men came from James’; rendered as Origen writes it. Galatians 2:9 is quoted loosely (Origen: ‘so that those two might preach to the Gentiles’; Paul: ‘that we should go to the Gentiles’); ‘those two’ renders the plural ἐκεῖνοι, which refers to Paul and Barnabas. ‘Israelite according to the flesh’ may echo 1 Corinthians 10:18 (‘Israel according to the flesh’); possible allusion only, not cited inline. Letter and spirit (‘from the law according to the letter to that according to the spirit’) may echo 2 Corinthians 3:6 or Romans 7:6; possible only. Acts 10:28 is cited for ‘looking down on those outside Judaism’ (Peter: ‘you know that it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with a foreigner’); Acts 21:21–26 for Paul’s offering (21:21 the charge of apostasy from Moses, 21:26 the offering). No LXX renumbering arises in this chapter.
